Re: Ayodhya Presidential Reference (1993) — SC's Refusal and Its Significance

shared.concept_anchor: Ayodhya 1993 — SC broadened grounds for refusal of reference

en.display_text:
The Presidential Reference in the Ayodhya matter (1993) is constitutionally significant primarily because:

(a) The Supreme Court declined the reference on the ground that the Attorney General had not endorsed the reference before it was formally transmitted, making the reference procedurally defective
(b) The Supreme Court declined the reference and, in doing so, extended the grounds for refusal under Article 143(a) beyond the hypothetical-question standard, articulating the broader test of whether answering would subserve national interest
(c) The Supreme Court declined the reference solely because questions involving communal or religious subjects form a constitutionally prohibited category under Article 143
(d) The Supreme Court declined the reference by applying the ratio of Re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, holding that the Ayodhya question constituted a live lis between identifiable parties
en.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall that 'communal sensitivity' was the reason for refusal in the Ayodhya reference may select (c), thinking the SC formulated a new test based solely on 'communal character of the question' — overlooking the broader 'national interest' formulation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Ayodhya reference was not declined because of a lack of the Attorney General's recommendation — no such procedural requirement exists.
Eliminate (c): While communal sensitivity was a factor, the SC's ratio was broader — it used the 'would not subserve national interest' formulation, which is wider than communal sensitivity alone.
Eliminate (d): Re: Cauvery's ratio was about live lis — not applicable to the Ayodhya reference, which was a historical-religious question, not an active inter-State dispute.

Confirm (b): Re: Ayodhya extended the grounds for refusal beyond Re: Kerala Education Bill's hypothetical-question test to include 'question would not subserve national interest,' thereby broadening the SC's discretion under Article 143(a).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here is between Re: Kerala Education Bill (1958) and Re: Ayodhya (1993). Students who know that 'hypothetical question' is a ground for refusal from Re: Kerala Education Bill may confuse which case added the 'national interest' test. Option (c) — communal sensitivity as a standalone test — is a partial-truth trap: communal sensitivity was cited but the formal legal test articulated was 'would not subserve national interest,' which is broader.
en.final_explanation:
Re: Ayodhya Presidential Reference (1993) is constitutionally significant not just for what it refused but for the broader test it articulated.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No provision requires the Attorney General to recommend a reference before it is made. The AG's role is post-reference — presenting it before the SC. Absence of AG endorsement has no legal consequence on the reference's validity.
• Option (b) — Correct: Re: Ayodhya (1993) broadened the grounds for the SC's refusal under Article 143(a) beyond the 'hypothetical question' standard of Re: Kerala Education Bill (1958). The SC formulated the 'would not subserve national interest' test, which is a wider, more flexible ground — allowing the SC to refuse politically or communally sensitive references even when they do not strictly qualify as 'hypothetical.'
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While communal sensitivity was a factor the SC emphasised, the formal ratio is the 'national interest' test — not a standalone 'communal character' test. The broader formulation is what matters constitutionally.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Re: Cauvery's ratio (live lis) was not applicable to the Ayodhya reference, which involved a historical-religious question, not an active legal dispute between parties over a legal right.

Value Addition:
• After Ayodhya (1993), the SC's discretion to refuse under 143(a) effectively encompasses: (i) hypothetical questions, (ii) live lis, (iii) insufficient public importance, and (iv) questions not subserving national interest.
• The reference was made by President Shankar Dayal Sharma on the advice of the Narasimha Rao government in 1993.
• The underlying Ayodhya title dispute was ultimately resolved by a Constitution Bench judgment in 2019.

hi.display_text:
अयोध्या मामले में राष्ट्रपति संदर्भ (1993) संवैधानिक रूप से महत्वपूर्ण है मुख्यतः क्योंकि:

(a) सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने संदर्भ को इसलिए अस्वीकार कर दिया क्योंकि अटॉर्नी जनरल ने संदर्भ को औपचारिक रूप से प्रेषित किए जाने से पहले अनुमोदित नहीं किया था, जिससे संदर्भ प्रक्रिया संबंधी दोषपूर्ण हो गया
(b) सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने संदर्भ को अस्वीकार कर दिया और ऐसा करते हुए, अनुच्छेद 143(a) के तहत अस्वीकृति के आधारों को काल्पनिक प्रश्न मानक से आगे बढ़ाया, व्यापक परीक्षण प्रस्तुत करते हुए कि उत्तर देना राष्ट्रीय हित की पूर्ति करेगा या नहीं
(c) सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने संदर्भ को केवल इसलिए अस्वीकार किया क्योंकि साम्प्रदायिक या धार्मिक विषयों वाले प्रश्न अनुच्छेद 143 के तहत संवैधानिक रूप से निषिद्ध श्रेणी बनाते हैं
(d) सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने संदर्भ को Re: कावेरी जल विवाद अधिकरण के अनुपात को लागू करते हुए अस्वीकार कर दिया, यह कहते हुए कि अयोध्या प्रश्न पहचान योग्य पक्षों के बीच जीवित विवाद था

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements about procedural aspects of advisory proceedings under Article 143 of the Constitution:

1. The Constitution of India does not specify any minimum quorum for the bench that must hear and decide an advisory reference under Article 143.
2. Advisory references under Article 143 must mandatorily be heard by a bench of at least seven judges, since they always involve substantial questions as to the interpretation of the Constitution.
3. Presidential references under Article 143 can include questions concerning service conditions and retirement age of constitutional functionaries.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution of India does not specify any minimum quorum for the bench that must hear and decide an advisory reference under Article 143.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike Article 145(c) which specifies a minimum five-judge bench for substantial questions of constitutional interpretation, there is no explicit quorum provision for advisory proceedings under Article 143.

statement_analysis.statement: Advisory references under Article 143 must mandatorily be heard by a bench of at least seven judges, since they always involve substantial questions as to the interpretation of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: No constitutional provision mandates a seven-judge bench for advisory references. The SC has discretion in constituting the bench, and not every advisory reference necessarily involves a substantial constitutional question requiring Article 145(c)'s five-judge minimum.

statement_analysis.statement: Presidential references under Article 143 can include questions concerning service conditions and retirement age of constitutional functionaries.
statement_analysis.reason: References can cover any question of law or fact of public importance — service conditions and retirement age of constitutional officers are matters of public importance, and precedents show such questions have been referred.

en.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Constitution Benches are associated with important constitutional questions may assume that advisory references — which deal with public importance matters — must always go to a seven-judge bench, making Statement 2 appear correct and leading them to select all-three-correct option (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — no explicit quorum provision exists for Article 143 advisory proceedings in the constitutional text.

Statement 2 claims a mandatory seven-judge bench — this is a plausible fabrication. Article 145(c) requires five judges for substantial constitutional questions, but no provision mandates seven judges for advisory references specifically.
Statement 3 is correct — advisory references on service conditions of constitutional functionaries are within the scope of Article 143's 'law or fact of public importance.'
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (a).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the association between important constitutional matters and larger Constitution Benches. Students who know that significant constitutional issues go to five-judge or seven-judge benches may apply this reasoning to advisory references, concluding that a seven-judge bench is always mandatory. In reality, there is no specific quorum provision for Article 143 proceedings — the Court has discretion in bench composition, and a five-judge bench (under Article 145(c) where a substantial constitutional question is involved) would be the floor, not a seven-judge mandatory bench.
en.final_explanation:
Article 143 is silent on bench composition and quorum — students must distinguish between what the Constitution specifies and what is merely conventional practice.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Constitution does not prescribe a minimum quorum for advisory references. Article 145(c) requires five judges for cases involving substantial questions as to the interpretation of the Constitution — this may apply to advisory references involving constitutional interpretation, but there is no separate, explicit quorum provision for Article 143 proceedings.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No provision mandates a seven-judge bench for all advisory references. This is a plausible-sounding fabrication. The bench size depends on the nature of the question — if it involves substantial constitutional interpretation, Article 145(c)'s five-judge minimum may apply, but seven is not a constitutional mandate.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Advisory references can cover any question of law or fact of public importance — including service conditions, retirement age, and other matters concerning constitutional functionaries. Such references have featured in Indian constitutional history.

Value Addition:
• Article 145(c) — minimum five-judge bench — applies to cases involving substantial questions of constitutional interpretation and may be triggered in advisory proceedings when such questions arise.
• The SC has internal administrative rules under Article 145 that govern bench constitution, but these are rules of practice, not constitutional mandates.
• The Chief Justice of India has discretion in constituting the bench for advisory proceedings.

shared.concept_anchor: Separation of powers — advisory jurisdiction debates

en.display_text:
Assertion (a): The exercise of advisory jurisdiction under Article 143, wherein the executive seeks an opinion from the Supreme Court, directly violates the separation of powers doctrine as recognised in the Indian Constitution.

Reason (R): Advisory proceedings under Article 143 do not involve the resolution of any dispute (lis) between parties — the Supreme Court renders an opinion rather than adjudicating a controversy between identifiable adversaries.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
en.strong_distractor: c — Students who know that advisory jurisdiction is constitutionally valid and has survived all challenges may incorrectly mark A as incorrect — believing that there is no 'significant separation of powers concern' since the SC has accepted advisory jurisdiction.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (a) correct? — No. Advisory jurisdiction has been subject to separation of powers critiques, but the SC has not held it unconstitutional or inconsistent with separation of powers. The concern exists academically, but the statement 'directly violates the separation of powers' is too strong — advisory jurisdiction has survived constitutional scrutiny. A is incorrect.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Advisory opinions under Article 143 do not resolve a lis between parties — they are non-adversarial opinions rendered in response to a presidential query. This is factually accurate.
Step 3: Since A is incorrect, the correct option cannot be (a) or (b). R is correct — correct option is (d).
A is incorrect but R is correct — correct option is (d).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is in Assertion (a)'s use of 'directly violates' — an extreme qualifier that makes an otherwise contested claim into a false absolute. The separation of powers concern about advisory jurisdiction is real and academically debated, but saying the exercise 'directly violates' the doctrine is an overstatement that makes A incorrect. Students who recognise the genuine tension between advisory jurisdiction and separation of powers may mark A as correct based on partial knowledge, selecting option (c) instead of (d).
en.final_explanation:
The relationship between Article 143 and the separation of powers doctrine is a nuanced constitutional debate.

Assertion (a) is incorrect: While it is true that scholars and critics have raised separation of powers arguments against advisory jurisdiction (the executive seeking opinions from the judiciary could blur institutional boundaries), the Supreme Court has NOT held that advisory jurisdiction directly violates the separation of powers. In Re: Delhi Laws Act (1951), the SC characterised advisory jurisdiction as a constitutional duty of a distinct character — implicitly accepting its constitutionality. The word 'directly violates' makes A an overstatement that is constitutionally inaccurate.

Reason (R) is correct: Advisory proceedings under Article 143 are non-adversarial — there is no lis between parties, no petitioner contesting against a respondent, and no binding resolution of a dispute. The SC renders an opinion, not a judgment on a controversy. This is factually accurate.

Since A is incorrect and R is correct — option (d).

Value Addition:
• The USA's prohibition on advisory opinions is explicitly grounded in separation of powers — federal courts need a 'case or controversy.' India chose a different constitutional design.
• Article 143 was part of the original Constitution — Parliament cannot expand or curtail it without constitutional amendment; a basic structure challenge would arise.
• The academic debate about advisory jurisdiction and separation of powers remains live — it is a standard topic in constitutional law scholarship.

hi.upsc_trap_explanation: फंदा कथन (a) में 'प्रत्यक्ष रूप से उल्लंघन करता है' के उपयोग में है — एक अत्यंत कठोर शब्द जो एक विवादित दावे को गलत पूर्णता में बदल देता है। सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार और शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के बीच वास्तविक और शैक्षणिक बहस है, लेकिन यह कहना कि यह अभ्यास 'प्रत्यक्ष रूप से उल्लंघन करता है' अतिशयोक्ति है जो A को गलत बनाती है। जो छात्र सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार और शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के बीच वास्तविक तनाव को पहचानते हैं, वे आंशिक ज्ञान के आधार पर A को सही चिह्नित कर सकते हैं, विकल्प (c) चुनते हुए बजाय (d) के।
hi.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 143 और शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के सिद्धांत के बीच संबंध एक सूक्ष्म संवैधानिक बहस है।

कथन (a) गलत है: जबकि यह सत्य है कि विद्वानों और आलोचकों ने सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार के खिलाफ शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के तर्क उठाए हैं (कार्यपालिका द्वारा न्यायपालिका से राय लेना संस्थागत सीमाओं को धुंधला कर सकता है), सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने यह नहीं माना कि सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार प्रत्यक्ष रूप से शक्तियों के पृथक्करण का उल्लंघन करता है। Re: Delhi Laws Act (1951) में, SC ने सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार को एक विशिष्ट संवैधानिक कर्तव्य के रूप में वर्णित किया — अप्रत्यक्ष रूप से इसकी संवैधानिकता को स्वीकार करते हुए। 'प्रत्यक्ष रूप से उल्लंघन करता है' शब्द A को अतिशयोक्ति बनाता है जो संवैधानिक रूप से गलत है।

कारण (R) सही है: अनुच्छेद 143 के तहत सलाहकार कार्यवाही गैर-विरोधात्मक होती है — पक्षों के बीच कोई विवाद (लिस) नहीं होता, कोई याचिकाकर्ता प्रतिवादी के विरुद्ध विवाद नहीं करता, और कोई बाध्यकारी विवाद समाधान नहीं होता। SC एक राय देता है, विवाद पर निर्णय नहीं। यह तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है।

चूंकि A गलत है और R सही है — विकल्प (d)।

Value Addition:
• अमेरिका में सलाहकार राय पर प्रतिबंध स्पष्ट रूप से शक्तियों के पृथक्करण में निहित है — संघीय न्यायालयों को 'मामला या विवाद' चाहिए। भारत ने एक अलग संवैधानिक डिजाइन चुना।
• अनुच्छेद 143 मूल संविधान का हिस्सा था — संसद इसे संवैधानिक संशोधन के बिना बढ़ा या घटा नहीं सकती; एक मूल संरचना चुनौती उत्पन्न होगी।
• सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार और शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के बारे में शैक्षणिक बहस जीवित है — यह संवैधानिक कानून के अध्ययन में एक मानक विषय है।

Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in terms of a presidential advisory reference and its specific outcome or doctrinal contribution?

(a) Re: Kerala Education Bill (1958) — Supreme Court declined the reference on the ground that the matter involved a live inter-State dispute more appropriately resolved through original jurisdiction
(b) Re: Delhi Laws Act (1951) — Supreme Court laid down the procedure for participation of amicus curiae in advisory proceedings and the public importance test for admissibility
(c) Re: Special Courts Bill (1978) — Supreme Court rendered a conditional advisory opinion upholding the validity of special courts, which directly influenced the final form of the enacted legislation
(d) Re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992) — Supreme Court declined the reference on the ground that the question was hypothetical and lacked sufficient public importance
en.strong_distractor: a — Pairing Re: Kerala Education Bill with 'declining a reference involving a live inter-State water dispute' is deceptive because students may confuse the two refusal cases (Kerala Education Bill vs Cauvery) — both involving the SC declining but on different grounds.

Re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992) — declined because of a live inter-State water dispute (live lis), not because the question was hypothetical. Option (d) is incorrectly matched.

Re: Kerala Education Bill (1958) — the SC in this case: (i) established that hypothetical questions may be declined, (ii) laid down that procedure resembles regular hearings with amicus curiae, and (iii) articulated the public importance test. These are all contributions of Re: Kerala Education Bill. Option (a) incorrectly pairs this case with Cauvery's ratio.

Students who know that Kerala Education Bill involved a refusal issue may not remember the precise ground (hypothetical/public importance, not live lis) and may select option (a) as correctly matched. Distinguishing between the grounds for refusal in Kerala Education Bill and Cauvery is the precise knowledge tested here.

Kerala Education Bill's contributions were: the public importance test, the procedure-resembles-regular-hearing principle, and the hypothetical-question refusal ground.

The SC gave a conditional advisory opinion upholding validity — and this opinion directly shaped the final form of the enacted legislation. This case illustrates how advisory opinions can blur into quasi-binding instruments.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992) declined because the matter was a live inter-State dispute (live lis), not because the question was hypothetical.

• The distinction between 'hypothetical question' (Kerala Education Bill) and 'live lis' (Cauvery) as grounds for refusal is a high-frequency UPSC precision test.
• Re: Special Courts Bill is the only major advisory reference where the SC's conditional opinion became the template for final legislation.
• Re: Ayodhya (1993) added a third ground: 'would not subserve national interest.'

shared.concept_anchor: India vs Canada — advisory opinion binding character comparison

en.display_text:
Consider two constitutional democracies: Country X and Country Y. In Country X, the apex court renders advisory opinions in response to executive reference on questions of public importance — these opinions are constitutionally recognised but are not legally binding on the executive or legislature, carrying only persuasive authority. In Country Y, the apex court similarly renders advisory opinions on executive reference, but these opinions are by constitutional convention treated as binding on the executive and legislature.

Which of the following correctly identifies Country X and Country Y?

(a) Country X — Canada; Country Y — India
(b) Country X — India; Country Y — Canada
(c) Country X — Canada; Country Y — Australia
(d) Country X — India; Country Y — USA
en.strong_distractor: a — Students who know India has advisory jurisdiction may assume India and Canada function identically, selecting option (a) — the 'both binding' option — without recalling that India's opinions are persuasive while Canada's are binding by convention.
elimination_logic: Country X: advisory opinions are constitutionally recognised and rendered by the apex court but are persuasive, not binding — this matches India (Article 143, non-binding advisory opinions).

Country Y: advisory opinions are recognised and by constitutional convention treated as binding on the executive and legislature — this matches Canada (Supreme Court of Canada Act reference jurisdiction, binding by convention).
Eliminate (a): Country X's opinions are not binding — India's are explicitly non-binding.
Eliminate (c) and (d): These incorrectly assign the binding/non-binding character. Option (b) — Country X is India and Country Y is Canada — is the only correct identification.
en.final_explanation:
This scenario tests whether students can map the theoretical comparative law knowledge to specific jurisdictions based on the defining operational difference.

Country X: Advisory opinions are constitutionally recognised and rendered by the apex court in response to executive reference but are explicitly non-binding — the executive may disregard them legally, though this is politically rare. This is India's position under Article 143.

Country Y: Advisory opinions are also rendered by the apex court on executive reference but are treated as binding by constitutional convention — in practice, the executive and legislature consider themselves bound by the opinion. This is Canada's position under the Supreme Court of Canada Act.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This would require both countries' opinions to be binding — incorrect for Country X (India), where opinions are non-binding.
• Option (b) — Correct: Country X = India (persuasive, non-binding) and Country Y = Canada (binding by convention). This captures the key distinction accurately.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Reversing the identification — Country X as Canada and Country Y as India — would reverse the binding/non-binding attribution.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: USA has no advisory jurisdiction at all — it cannot be Country Y, which renders advisory opinions.

Value Addition:
• In Re: Secession of Quebec (1998), Canada's advisory opinion by the Supreme Court on the legality of unilateral secession is a landmark example of an advisory opinion with enormous constitutional consequence.
• India's advisory jurisdiction was influenced by the Canadian model via the Government of India Act, 1935.
• The non-binding nature of India's advisory opinions arguably gives the SC more freedom to render candid opinions without fear of direct political consequences.

hi.display_text:
दो संवैधानिक लोकतंत्रों पर विचार करें: देश X और देश Y। देश X में, सर्वोच्च न्यायालय कार्यपालिका के संदर्भ पर सार्वजनिक महत्व के प्रश्नों पर सलाहकार राय देता है — ये राय संवैधानिक रूप से मान्यता प्राप्त हैं लेकिन कार्यपालिका या विधायिका पर कानूनी रूप से बाध्यकारी नहीं हैं, केवल प्रेरक अधिकारिता रखती हैं। देश Y में, सर्वोच्च न्यायालय इसी प्रकार कार्यपालिका के संदर्भ पर सलाहकार राय देता है, लेकिन ये राय संवैधानिक परंपरा द्वारा कार्यपालिका और विधायिका पर बाध्यकारी मानी जाती हैं।

निम्नलिखित में से कौन-सा विकल्प देश X और देश Y की सही पहचान करता है?

(a) देश X — कनाडा; देश Y — भारत
(b) देश X — भारत; देश Y — कनाडा
(c) देश X — कनाडा; देश Y — ऑस्ट्रेलिया
(d) देश X — भारत; देश Y — अमेरिका
hi.strong_distractor: a — जो छात्र जानते हैं कि भारत के पास सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार है, वे मान सकते हैं कि भारत और कनाडा समान रूप से कार्य करते हैं, और विकल्प (a) — 'दोनों बाध्यकारी' विकल्प — चुन सकते हैं, बिना यह याद किए कि भारत की राय प्रेरक हैं जबकि कनाडा की परंपरा द्वारा बाध्यकारी हैं।
elimination_logic: देश X: सलाहकार राय संवैधानिक रूप से मान्यता प्राप्त हैं और सर्वोच्च न्यायालय द्वारा दी जाती हैं लेकिन प्रेरक हैं, बाध्यकारी नहीं — यह भारत से मेल खाता है (अनुच्छेद 143, गैर-बाध्यकारी सलाहकार राय)।

देश Y: सलाहकार राय मान्यता प्राप्त हैं और संवैधानिक परंपरा द्वारा कार्यपालिका और विधायिका पर बाध्यकारी मानी जाती हैं — यह कनाडा से मेल खाता है (Supreme Court of Canada Act संदर्भ क्षेत्राधिकार, परंपरा द्वारा बाध्यकारी)।
विकल्प (a) को हटाएं: देश X की राय बाध्यकारी नहीं हैं — भारत की राय स्पष्ट रूप से गैर-बाध्यकारी हैं।
विकल्प (c) और (d) को हटाएं: ये बाध्यकारी/गैर-बाध्यकारी चरित्र को गलत रूप से सौंपते हैं। विकल्प (b) — देश X भारत है और देश Y कनाडा है — ही सही पहचान है।
hi.final_explanation:
यह परिदृश्य यह परीक्षण करता है कि छात्र सैद्धांतिक तुलनात्मक विधि ज्ञान को विशिष्ट क्षेत्राधिकारों के साथ परिभाषित परिचालन अंतर के आधार पर मैप कर सकते हैं या नहीं।

देश X: सलाहकार राय संवैधानिक रूप से मान्यता प्राप्त हैं और कार्यपालिका के संदर्भ पर सर्वोच्च न्यायालय द्वारा दी जाती हैं लेकिन स्पष्ट रूप से गैर-बाध्यकारी हैं — कार्यपालिका इन्हें कानूनी रूप से नजरअंदाज कर सकती है, हालांकि यह राजनीतिक रूप से दुर्लभ है। यह भारत की स्थिति है अनुच्छेद 143 के तहत।

देश Y: सलाहकार राय भी कार्यपालिका के संदर्भ पर सर्वोच्च न्यायालय द्वारा दी जाती हैं लेकिन संवैधानिक परंपरा द्वारा बाध्यकारी मानी जाती हैं — व्यवहार में, कार्यपालिका और विधायिका स्वयं को राय द्वारा बाध्य मानते हैं। यह कनाडा की स्थिति है Supreme Court of Canada Act के तहत।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: इसके लिए दोनों देशों की राय बाध्यकारी होनी चाहिए — देश X (भारत) के लिए गलत, जहाँ राय गैर-बाध्यकारी हैं।
• विकल्प (b) — सही: देश X = भारत (प्रेरक, गैर-बाध्यकारी) और देश Y = कनाडा (परंपरा द्वारा बाध्यकारी)। यह मुख्य अंतर को सही ढंग से दर्शाता है।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: पहचान उलट देना — देश X को कनाडा और देश Y को भारत मानना — बाध्यकारी/गैर-बाध्यकारी वर्गीकरण को उलट देगा।

Value Addition:
• Re: Secession of Quebec (1998) में, कनाडा की सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की सलाहकार राय, जो एकतरफा पृथक्करण की वैधता पर थी, एक महत्वपूर्ण उदाहरण है जिसमें सलाहकार राय का विशाल संवैधानिक प्रभाव था।

Assertion (a): State governments may participate and be heard in advisory proceedings under Article 143 even though they are not formal parties to any dispute before the Supreme Court.

Reason (R): Article 131 of the Constitution grants State governments the right to participate in any Supreme Court proceeding that substantially affects their interests, including advisory references made by the President.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
en.strong_distractor: a — Students may quickly accept (a) since both A and R appear factually connected — 'States can be heard because there is no formal lis' seems like a natural causal chain.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (a) correct? — Yes. State governments can participate and be heard in advisory proceedings under Article 143 even though they are not formal parties to any lis.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. R states that 'Article 131 grants State governments the right to participate in any Supreme Court proceeding that affects their interests.' Article 131 is the SC's original jurisdiction for inter-State disputes — it does not grant States a general right to participate in all SC proceedings. This is a factual inaccuracy.
Step 3: Since R is incorrect, the only applicable option is (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.
A is correct, R is incorrect — correct option is (c).
en.final_explanation:
This question tests whether students carefully verify the factual accuracy of R rather than accepting a plausible-sounding causal explanation.

Assertion (a) is correct: In advisory proceedings under Article 143, State governments may be heard and may participate even though there is no formal lis and they are not parties to any dispute. The SC regularly invites or permits State governments to file submissions and make oral arguments in advisory proceedings because the referred questions often have significant federal implications.

Reason (R) is incorrect: Article 131 is the Supreme Court's exclusive original jurisdiction for disputes between the Union and States or between States — it does not create a general right for States to participate in any SC proceeding affecting their interests. The basis for State participation in Article 143 proceedings is the SC's own discretion and procedural practice, not any right derived from Article 131. R misattributes the source of State participation to Article 131, making R factually inaccurate.

Since A is correct but R is incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• States have a strong practical interest in advisory proceedings on federal questions — Centre-State fiscal relations, legislative competence, Concurrent List disputes — even without formal party status.
• The SC's discretion to admit States as participants in advisory proceedings reflects the broader 'interested party' model unique to advisory jurisdiction.
• Article 131's scope is specifically limited to actual inter-governmental disputes — it is not a broad participatory right.

shared.concept_anchor: Constitutional safeguard — SC discretion prevents misuse of Article 143

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements about constitutional propriety and the potential for misuse of Article 143:

1. The Supreme Court's discretion to refuse a reference under Article 143(a) operates as a constitutional safeguard against potential misuse of the advisory jurisdiction for political purposes.
2. Once the President makes a reference under Article 143(a), the Supreme Court is constitutionally obligated to hear it and render an opinion; any refusal by the SC would amount to an unconstitutional dereliction of its constitutional duty.
3. The constitutional propriety debate around Article 143 raises the concern that a politically motivated reference could allow the executive to obtain judicial imprimatur for a policy position — blurring institutional boundaries.

Which of the above statements is/are NOT correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 2 and 3 only

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court's discretion to refuse a reference under Article 143(a) operates as a constitutional safeguard against potential misuse of the advisory jurisdiction for political purposes.
statement_analysis.reason: The SC's refusal power under 143(a) — as exercised in Re: Ayodhya (1993) — is precisely the mechanism that prevents the executive from using advisory references to gain judicial endorsement for politically motivated questions.

statement_analysis.statement: Once the President makes a reference under Article 143(a), the Supreme Court is constitutionally obligated to hear it and render an opinion; any refusal by the SC would amount to an unconstitutional dereliction of its constitutional duty.
statement_analysis.reason: This is wrong on both counts: (i) Article 143(a) uses 'may' — the SC has discretion to decline; (ii) declining a reference under 143(a) is not a 'dereliction of duty' — it is a constitutionally sanctioned exercise of discretion established in Re: Kerala Education Bill and Re: Ayodhya.

statement_analysis.statement: The constitutional propriety debate around Article 143 raises the concern that a politically motivated reference could allow the executive to obtain judicial imprimatur for a policy position — blurring institutional boundaries.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately captures the constitutional propriety concern — advisory jurisdiction could theoretically be misused to obtain judicial backing for executive positions, raising separation of powers concerns.

en.strong_distractor: d — Students may mark Statement 3 as incorrect, thinking it overstates the concern about advisory jurisdiction misuse — especially if they recall that the SC has effectively handled such concerns through its refusal power.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — SC's refusal discretion under 143(a) is the built-in constitutional safeguard against misuse. Not incorrect.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 143(a) uses 'may,' not 'shall.' Refusal under 143(a) is constitutionally sanctioned, not a dereliction of duty. This is the NOT-correct statement.
Statement 3 is correct — the concern about executive-judicial boundary blurring through politically motivated references is a genuine and recognised constitutional propriety debate.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option (b).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension in Statement 2 converts a conditional discretion ('may refuse') into an absolute obligation ('shall render opinion or else it is unconstitutional dereliction'). Students who recall the general principle that 'the SC must take up its constitutional duties' may not notice that this specific duty under 143(a) is discretionary — and that exercising the discretion to refuse is itself a constitutional act, not a dereliction. The words 'unconstitutional dereliction' are the tells.
en.final_explanation:
Statements 1 and 3 describe the constitutional debate around Article 143 accurately. Statement 2 is the problematic one.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The SC's discretion to refuse under Article 143(a) is the primary constitutional safeguard against politically motivated references. The Re: Ayodhya (1993) refusal is the clearest illustration — the SC exercised this discretion to prevent judicial involvement in a communally sensitive political question.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (NOT correct): This statement creates a false obligation. Article 143(a) uses 'may report' — the SC has discretion, not a mandatory duty. Refusing a reference under 143(a) on grounds of lack of public importance, hypothetical character, or national interest is a constitutionally legitimate act, not a dereliction of duty. The mandatory obligation ('shall report') exists only under Article 143(b).
• Statement 3 — Correct: The constitutional propriety concern — that advisory references could be used by the executive to obtain judicial backing for a political position — is a recognised debate in constitutional scholarship. This concern motivated both the Re: Ayodhya refusal and academic critiques of the advisory jurisdiction framework.

Value Addition:
• The SC's refusal power under 143(a) is a stronger institutional safeguard than exists in Canada, where advisory opinions are binding — Canada's SC has less freedom to decline.
• The India-Canada comparison is instructive: India's non-binding + discretion-to-decline model gives the SC more independence than Canada's binding + convention-bound model.
• Parliamentary sovereignty and judicial independence both require that the SC retain the freedom to refuse inappropriate references.

elimination_logic: कथन 1 सही है — 143(a) के तहत SC का अस्वीकार करने का विवेकाधिकार दुरुपयोग के विरुद्ध अंतर्निहित संवैधानिक सुरक्षा है। यह गलत नहीं है।
कथन 2 गलत है — अनुच्छेद 143(a) में 'may' शब्द का प्रयोग है, 'shall' का नहीं। 143(a) के तहत अस्वीकार करना संवैधानिक रूप से अनुमोदित है, कर्तव्य की उपेक्षा नहीं। यह NOT-सही कथन है।
कथन 3 सही है — राजनीतिक प्रेरित संदर्भों के माध्यम से कार्यपालिका-न्यायिक सीमाओं के धुंधले होने की चिंता एक वास्तविक और मान्यता प्राप्त संवैधानिक शुद्धता बहस है।
केवल कथन 2 सही नहीं है — विकल्प (b)।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: कथन 2 में दायरा-विस्तार एक सशर्त विवेकाधिकार ('अस्वीकार कर सकता है') को एक पूर्ण बाध्यता ('राय देनी होगी या फिर यह संवैधानिक कर्तव्य की उपेक्षा है') में बदल देता है। जो छात्र सामान्य सिद्धांत याद रखते हैं कि 'SC को अपने संवैधानिक कर्तव्यों को निभाना चाहिए' वे यह नहीं देख पाते कि 143(a) के तहत यह विशिष्ट कर्तव्य विवेकाधिकारयुक्त है — और अस्वीकार करने का विवेकाधिकार प्रयोग करना स्वयं एक संवैधानिक कार्य है, कर्तव्य की उपेक्षा नहीं। 'अवैध उपेक्षा' शब्द इस बात का संकेत हैं।
hi.final_explanation:
कथन 1 और 3 अनुच्छेद 143 के आसपास संवैधानिक बहस को सही ढंग से वर्णित करते हैं। कथन 2 समस्या उत्पन्न करता है।

• कथन 1 — सही: अनुच्छेद 143(a) के तहत SC का अस्वीकार करने का विवेकाधिकार राजनीतिक प्रेरित संदर्भों के विरुद्ध मुख्य संवैधानिक सुरक्षा है। Re: अयोध्या (1993) में अस्वीकार करना इसका स्पष्ट उदाहरण है — SC ने इस विवेकाधिकार का प्रयोग एक सांप्रदायिक संवेदनशील राजनीतिक प्रश्न में न्यायिक भागीदारी को रोकने के लिए किया।
• कथन 2 — गलत (NOT सही): यह कथन एक गलत बाध्यता बनाता है। अनुच्छेद 143(a) में 'may report' शब्द है — SC के पास विवेकाधिकार है, अनिवार्य कर्तव्य नहीं। सार्वजनिक महत्व की कमी, काल्पनिक स्वभाव, या राष्ट्रीय हित के आधार पर 143(a) के तहत संदर्भ अस्वीकार करना संवैधानिक रूप से वैध कार्य है, कर्तव्य की उपेक्षा नहीं। अनिवार्य कर्तव्य ('shall report') केवल अनुच्छेद 143(b) के तहत है।
• कथन 3 — सही: संवैधानिक शुद्धता की चिंता — कि सलाहकार संदर्भ कार्यपालिका को राजनीतिक स्थिति के लिए न्यायिक समर्थन प्राप्त करने के लिए उपयोग किया जा सकता है — संवैधानिक विद्वता में मान्यता प्राप्त बहस है। इस चिंता ने Re: अयोध्या अस्वीकार और सलाहकार क्षेत्राधिकार के ढांचे की अकादमिक आलोचनाओं को प्रेरित किया।

Value Addition:
• 143(a) के तहत SC की अस्वीकार करने की शक्ति कनाडा की तुलना में अधिक मजबूत संस्थागत सुरक्षा है, जहां सलाहकार राय बाध्यकारी होती हैं — कनाडा का SC अस्वीकार करने की कम स्वतंत्रता रखता है।
• भारत-कनाडा तुलना शिक्षाप्रद है: भारत का गैर-बाध्यकारी + अस्वीकार करने का विवेकाधिकार मॉडल SC को कनाडा के बाध्यकारी + परंपरा-बंधित मॉडल की तुलना में अधिक स्वतंत्रता देता है।
• संसदीय संप्रभुता और न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता दोनों यह आवश्यक बनाते हैं कि SC अनुचित संदर्भों को अस्वीकार करने की स्वतंत्रता बनाए रखे।
